title: Fragmentation / repeated low-value purchase risk pattern
learning_objectives: Apply estimated-value reasoning to similar needs
Assess documentation gaps and audit-trail quality
Evaluate when internal verification or escalation is needed
red_flags: Similar needs framed as isolated low-value purchases
Multiple units requesting related supplies in the same period
Separate market research memos used instead of combined review
Post-facto justification after risk indicators appear

n1.text: A hospital department has several similar supply needs during the same financial year. Different units propose separate low-value purchases from the same supplier family.
n1.challenge: Which option best addresses the fragmentation risk and creates the strongest audit trail without causing undue operational delays?

A.text: Proceed with separate purchases immediately but document the urgent need.
A.feedback: Option A is fast, but it treats similar needs as isolated requests. This may weaken estimated-value reasoning and create a weak audit trail.
A.expert_log: Chose isolated requests over consolidation. Increased audit risk.

B.text: Consolidate the requests to assess the total estimated value before proceeding.
B.feedback: Option B is the strongest response. It consolidates similar needs for review, supports estimated-value reasoning, and creates a clearer audit trail before any award decision.

C.text: Ask each unit to provide a separate market research memo, then process them individually.
C.feedback: Option C improves documentation at unit level, but separate memos do not fully address the fragmentation risk if the needs are similar and should be examined together.
C.expert_log: Chose separate memos. Marginal documentation improvement but fragmentation risk remains.

n2.text: The separate purchases proceed, but internal tracking flags that the combined volume of these isolated requests may exceed the scope suitable for isolated handling.
n2.challenge: How do you rectify the audit finding?

A.text: Argue the needs were unforeseeable to justify the isolated handling.
A.feedback: Arguing unforeseeability post-facto for routine supplies creates a severe audit vulnerability.

B.text: Consolidate the remaining needs to assess their total scope.
B.feedback: Consolidating remaining needs shows corrective action and mitigates further risk.

C.text: Cancel all remaining requests to avoid further exposure.
C.feedback: Canceling operational needs entirely harms the hospital's core mission.
C.expert_log: Operational risk induced to avoid audit tracking.

n3.text: The consolidated estimated value is calculated and confirms it requires broader review beyond standard low-value workflows.
n3.challenge: What is the most appropriate next step?

A.text: Escalate the request for a more structured supplier comparison route.
A.feedback: Escalating for a structured supplier comparison is the proper action for aggregated values.
A.expert_log: Correct escalation for structured comparison initiated.

B.text: Split the value between two different financial years to avoid broader review.
B.feedback: Splitting across financial years to evade broader review is a classic fragmentation indicator and severely increases audit risk.
B.expert_log: Attempted deliberate fragmentation across financial years.

C.text: Seek expanded market research to justify the combined value.
C.feedback: Seeking expanded market research supports value-for-money reasoning and a clearer evidence trail.

n4.text: Market research suggests only two suitable suppliers are immediately available for the consolidated volume.
n4.challenge: How do you handle the limited supplier availability?

A.text: Proceed with comparing only the two identified suppliers to save time.
A.feedback: Comparing only two suppliers offers minimal assurance of value-for-money, but may be acceptable if thoroughly justified.
A.expert_log: Proceeded with minimum comparison. Marginal value-for-money risk.

B.text: Expand the search or escalate for a broader review.
B.feedback: Expanding the search supports strong transparency safeguards and value-for-money.

C.text: Ask the suppliers directly to lower prices based on the larger volume.
C.feedback: Informal price negotiation without a structured comparison process creates probity and transparency risks.

n5.text: The internal review team suggests internal verification against applicable rules before finalizing the structured comparison.
n5.challenge: How should the procurement team respond?

A.text: Support internal verification against applicable rules and ensure documentation is complete.
A.feedback: Supporting verification ensures a highly defensible audit trail and minimal risk.
A.expert_log: Supported internal verification. Strong audit defensibility.

B.text: Push back on the review to prioritize operational speed.
B.feedback: Bypassing internal review prioritizes speed but increases exposure to audit findings.

C.text: Delegate the review back to the requesting units.
C.feedback: Delegating centralized review back to the units creates circular delays and weakens oversight.

n6.text: Severe risk indicators are present: administrative burden is rising, and the audit trail lacks a cohesive justification.
n6.challenge: What is the final corrective action?

A.text: Stop the current approach and redesign the request centrally.
A.feedback: Redesigning centrally is costly in time but effectively mitigates severe audit risk.
A.expert_log: Halted process for central redesign. High time cost, safe audit.

B.text: Justify past actions in a single overarching memo and proceed.
B.feedback: A single memo cannot retroactively cure systemic fragmentation or transparency flaws.
B.expert_log: Relied on weak post-facto memo justification.

C.text: Accept operational delay and postpone the needs until the next planning cycle.
C.feedback: Postponing resolves the audit risk but represents a failure to meet operational needs.
C.expert_log: Accepted operational failure to avoid audit risk.
